title: Revisiting Modularity Maximization for Graph Clustering: A Contrastive Learning Perspective

problem.claim: Graph clustering aims to classify graph nodes into disjoint clusters.

gap.claim: The underlying mechanism of modularity maximization for graph clustering is not well understood.

contributions.claim: The work analyzes the hidden success of modularity maximization for graph clustering.
The analysis identifies strong connections between modularity maximization and graph contrastive learning, with modularity naturally defining positive and negative examples.
The work proposes a community-aware graph clustering framework, øurs, that uses modularity maximization as a contrastive pretext task to uncover community information while avoiding semantic drift.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on multiple graph datasets are reported to verify øurs's scalability and clustering performance compared with state-of-the-art graph clustering methods.
The authors report that øurs scales to a graph with 100M nodes while outperforming strong baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Graph clustering is a fundamental graph-mining task, and graph contrastive learning has become a dominant approach.
Graph contrastive learning depends heavily on augmentations and contrastive schemes that may cause semantic drift and scalability issues.
Modularity maximization is presented as a promising clustering principle, but its underlying mechanism remains poorly understood.
The work connects modularity maximization with graph contrastive learning and proposes øurs as a community-aware framework based on modularity-derived contrastive examples.
The authors report improved scalability and clustering performance, including scaling to a 100M-node graph while outperforming strong baselines.

source_observation.claim: Modularity can naturally define positive and negative examples for graph contrastive learning.

interpretation.claim: A domain objective may provide contrastive structure without relying exclusively on manually designed graph augmentations.

application.claim: For graph clustering, investigate community or structural objectives as contrastive pretext tasks.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this approach avoids semantic drift across graph types or datasets beyond the reported experiments.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, or experimental protocols.
The abstract does not explain the framework architecture or optimization procedure.
The abstract does not provide quantitative performance results or resource requirements.
